title: Why Duke wrote clashing chords for the Basie session and avoided a band battle
summary: Duke's tension chords were deliberate, and he kept the joint session from becoming a contest.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Do you think Duke did things like that psychologically, writing the music in a way that would affect the players?
Like what, could you give me an example?
Well, I was -- let me see. I'm going to go back -- this was a collective situation, on the Basie and Duke.
Did you write some of that stuff?

No, I didn't. I didn't know they were recording that day. I think Bud Johnson called me up and told me to come over to Columbia Record studios. But I think when Duke wrote those clashes, when I said that Marshall Royal said he was splitting atoms?

He did that on purpose, because Basie plays kind of pure, you know. There's a difference -- but they sound good playing it. It's just that the -- Ellington just wrote that way. And okay, now there was -- of course there's going to be some competitive feeling, even though Duke and Basie were tight. But the pride that the guy has in his craft.

Two of the best bands. So Duke would write those high tension chords, and I think that's one of the reasons why he would -- like I was saying, Thad Jones would play, and his reed section would play behind Thad.
He would never let it get to a contest. That's the reason it came out that way, you know?
Well, he would never play a so-called battle of the bands.
